title: Zigzag Iterator
statement:
Write an iterator `ZigzagIterator` over two integer lists `v1` and `v2` that hands out their values alternately: the first value of `v1`, then the first of `v2`, then the second of `v1`, the second of `v2`, and so on. Once one list is used up, the remaining values of the other list follow in their original order.

- `new ZigzagIterator(v1, v2)` sets up the iterator.
- `hasNext()` returns `true` while at least one value has not been returned yet, and `false` otherwise.
- `next()` returns the next value in that order. It is only called when a value is left.

The judge builds the iterator from `v1` and `v2`, then calls `next()` for as long as `hasNext()` returns `true`; the list of values it collects is your answer. Write `ZigzagIterator` as a class (or as a constructor function with `hasNext` and `next` on its prototype).
notes:
## Intuition

The simplest idea is to write out the whole zigzag order in the constructor and then walk it with a position, but that copies every value before the first call. A lazier design keeps only a small to-do list: which list should give the next value, and from which index. A queue fits that rotation exactly: take the front list, hand out one value, and if that list still has more, send it to the back. An empty list never enters the queue, so turns automatically skip it, and the same design works for any number of lists.

## Approach

1. In the constructor, push `[v1, 0]` and `[v2, 0]` onto `queue`, skipping any empty list.
2. `hasNext()` is `true` exactly while `queue` is not empty.
3. `next()` removes the front pair `[list, index]`.
4. If `list` has a value after `index`, push `[list, index + 1]` to the back so it waits for its next turn.
5. Return `list[index]`.

## Example 1, step by step

With `v1 = [1, 2]` and `v2 = [3, 4, 5, 6]`, `queue` starts as `[[v1, 0], [v2, 0]]`. The calls return `1` (v1 goes to the back at index 1), `3` (v2 goes back at index 1), `2` (v1 is finished and is dropped), then `4`, `5` and `6` from v2 alone. After `6`, `queue` is empty, `hasNext()` is `false`, and the collected answer is `[1, 3, 2, 4, 5, 6]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) per call; the queue never holds more than two pairs, so `shift()` is constant here (O(k) for k lists).
- Space: O(1) extra: the iterator stores positions, not copies of the lists.

## Pitfalls

- An empty `v1` or `v2` must not take a turn; leaving it out of the queue handles that.
- After the shorter list ends, the rest of the longer list must come out in order, not stop early.
- `hasNext()` must not move the iterator; only `next()` changes the queue.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `queue` | pairs `[list, index]` waiting for their turn, front goes next |
| `list` | the list whose turn it is |
| `index` | position of the value `list` hands out now |

narration.3: The queue holds one [list, index] pair per list that still has values, in turn order.
narration.4: v1 goes first, starting at index 0, but only if it has any values.
narration.5: v2 takes the second turn, again only if it is not empty.
narration.9: There is a next value exactly when some list is still waiting in the queue.
narration.13: Take the list whose turn it is and the index of its next value.
narration.14: Does this list have another value after this one?
narration.15: Yes: send it to the back of the queue so the other list goes first.
narration.17: Hand out the value at the current position.
